[chip: Medium +1] Its central question is something like this: What happens when a poet becomes not just the writer of poems, but a whole universe of writers, historical figures, voices, and imagined identities? What does “heteronym compendium” mean? A heteronym is more than a pen name. In the tradition of the Portuguese poet Fernando Pessoa, a heteronym is a distinct literary personality, potentially with its own worldview, voice, style, and imagined biography. A compendium gathers multiple such identities or bodies of work into one collection. In Antioch, Sharks takes this idea in an exuberant, sometimes deliberately chaotic direction. The book invokes an extraordinary range of figures, including Walt Whitman, Ezra Pound, Jesus Christ, Moses, Nietzsche, Tupac, Kurt Cobain, and characters from popular culture. Some are literary predecessors; others are religious, mythological, or contemporary cultural figures. The boundaries between historical influence, fictional persona, parody, and spiritual identification are deliberately unstable. [chip: Medium +1] The result is less like a conventional poetry anthology and more like a literary cosmos in which different voices can inhabit, challenge, and transform one another. Literary inheritance and the struggle with predecessors One of the book's most striking sections is The Secret Book of Walt, which revolves around Walt Whitman and the idea that a poet might inherit, embody, or even become another poet. Sharks's writing engages the legacy of American poetry while refusing to treat literary history as something safely confined to the past. The book also wrestles with Ezra Pound, whose importance to modernism is inseparable from the moral problems of his political beliefs. In Who Is Lee Sharks, to Forgive Ezra Pound?, literary inheritance becomes an ethical problem: what does it mean to carry the words of a compromised predecessor forward? [image card: Six days of creation - Hildegard of Bingen | Artera | AskArtera] 2. Religious revelation and Gnostic imagery The opening poem, HADITH with TEETH, presents an encounter with the angel Sariel. The speaker resists being told to repeat what has already been said, only to discover that repetition can make an ancient utterance new again. This establishes a central paradox: originality may not mean inventing something unprecedented. It may mean entering an inherited tradition so completely that its words become newly alive. Biblical figures, angels, salvation, damnation, death, and rebirth recur throughout the collection. Religious language becomes a way of exploring poetic creation, suffering, and the possibility of transformation. [chip: Medium +1] [image card: Kalos&Klio | Christos Kalos-Klio Tantalidis | Living Postcards - The new face of Greece] 3. High culture collides with pop culture Sharks places figures from classical philosophy, Christian theology, modernist literature, hip-hop, and children's entertainment in the same imaginative space. Names such as Socrates, Nietzsche, Kanye West, Tupac, Snoop Dogg, Rainbow Dash, and Optimus Prime appear within the book's expansive catalog of identities. This collision makes the work funny, disorienting, and difficult to classify. It refuses the idea that only traditionally prestigious subjects belong in serious poetry. At the same time, the accumulation of references can feel overwhelming rather than immediately illuminating. [image card: EmRes for Depression Recovery: Exploring the Multifaceted Nature of Depression] 4. The instability of the self The question of who is speaking runs through the entire project. Is the author Lee Sharks? Is a poem spoken through another literary personality? Can a writer meaningfully inhabit another writer's voice, or does that voice become something new in the process? Damascus Dancings is identified as a collaborating persona, while Jack Feist and other figures enter the book's elaborate network of identities. The title Antioch sits within a project where authorship is not simply a name on a cover; it is one of the subjects being explored. How is the book structured? The published text is unusually long for a poetry collection, running to thousands of lines. Its sections range across several different modes of writing rather than following a single narrative. [chip: Medium +1] Some notable sections include: “HADITH with TEETH” — a compact, intense opening meditation on repetition, revelation, and the transformation of inherited language. “The Secret Book of Walt” — an elaborate, comic and mythological reimagining of Walt Whitman and poetic succession. “I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z” — another major section concerned with poetic identity and the assumption of literary authority. “Decrepit Memoir” — a turn toward autobiographical and self-reflective writing. “concre(a)tion” and “to wrestle with an angel” — titles that suggest the book's interest in experimental form and spiritual struggle. “WHO IS LEE SHARKS, TO FORGIVE EZRA POUND?” — a particularly revealing exploration of authorship, literary guilt, historical memory, and the burden of influence. The work's scale is part of its aesthetic. It seems intent on building an entire literary mythology rather than delivering a neatly curated sequence of independent poems. What is distinctive about Lee Sharks's style? Three characteristics stand out in the available text. 1. Deliberate excess. Sharks piles up names, allusions, theological references, jokes, and extravagant claims. The writing often seems to expand faster than a reader can comfortably organize it. 2. Abrupt tonal shifts. A passage can move from biblical solemnity to absurdist comedy without warning. A grand account of cosmic or spiritual destiny might suddenly be interrupted by an incongruous pop-culture reference. The contrast is part of the experience. 3. A mixture of sincerity and self-parody. The religious language and references to salvation are often intensely earnest, while other passages expose the grandiosity of the poetic enterprise through absurdity. It is not always obvious where the visionary performance ends and the joke begins. These characteristics make the work potentially rewarding for readers who enjoy experimental, maximalist writing, but less accessible to someone looking for concise poems with clear arguments or conventional narrative development. How should you read it? I would recommend starting with “HADITH with TEETH” and then reading “The Secret Book of Walt” before attempting the entire collection. The opening poem gives you a useful interpretive key: the relationship between repetition and originality. From there, the Whitman section expands the problem into a much larger game involving literary inheritance, imagined history, and the multiplication of poetic identities. When reading, it helps to ask three questions: Who is speaking? Is this the author, a fictional persona, a historical figure being reimagined, or a deliberately unstable combination? What is being inherited? Is the poem drawing on a literary style, a religious tradition, a cultural icon, or the authority attached to a famous name? What does the excess accomplish? Does the accumulation of references create a meaningful connection, generate comic disorientation, or simply overwhelm the reader? You do not need to recognize every allusion to appreciate the book. Its central concerns are often legible even when individual references are not. My assessment Antioch: A Heteronym Compendium is most interesting as an experiment in poetry as a system of identities, influences, and competing claims to authorship. Its ambition is not merely to write poems about other writers. It attempts to create a world in which literary history, religious mythology, popular culture, and the author's own identity become interconnected parts of a single imaginative structure. That ambition is also its main risk. The abundance of references and the sheer scale of the work can make it difficult to distinguish a carefully developed poetic insight from an accumulating private mythology. The text's grand declarations are part of its character, but they are not necessarily proof of artistic success. The best way to judge it is to examine how effectively particular passages turn their ideas into compelling language. For readers interested in experimental poetry, Whitman, Pessoa-style heteronyms, religious symbolism, and the strange relationship between literary influence and personal identity, it offers a great deal to investigate. The central tension is this: Can a poet become many voices without losing the ability to speak as a self? And can inherited words become genuinely new without pretending they came from nowhere? Those questions make Antioch more than a collection of eccentric references. They provide a way into its sprawling and often deliberately bewildering poetic universe. Its two statements suggest that both illumination and directness involve some kind of sacrifice or concealment. The title Hymn places these statements in a devotional register, but the speaker's devotion is directed toward the difficult conditions of writing itself. Its opening section connects breath, bodily exhaustion, and the physical presence of words on a page. The second section imagines the reader's eventual death and preservation; the third describes the speaker's continued existence as dependent on the reader's act of reading. [chip: Medium] The poem's central reversal is that the dead text needs the living reader as much as the living reader needs the text. The speaker is not simply a dead person speaking from beyond the grave. The poem repeatedly makes its own material existence part of the situation: words are preserved, but they need to be breathed in again. Reading becomes a kind of respiration. Notice, too, how the poem's imagery refuses to separate preservation from decay. A body becomes a specimen in a glass case; a grave becomes a sign; a voice accumulates residue. The text imagines immortality not as escaping material existence but as continuing through imperfect material forms. The question posed near the end of the second section—whether the reader can doubt their own immortality—therefore has a peculiar force. The apocalypse is not simply an external catastrophe. It's also a condition of attention. It moves from the relationship between words and silence to the speaker's internal possession of Ezra Pound, before arriving at the question in the title. [chip: Medium +1] Three movements are worth tracking. “They carry me.” The speaker says of Pound's words, after declaring that he carries them around. The grammatical reversal matters: influence is not merely something the living writer does to the dead writer's language. The inherited language also carries and constitutes the living writer. “Ez Pound tells me things, and I forgive him, over and over.” Forgiveness becomes repetitive, almost a ritual of literary inheritance. The poem doesn't let the ethical problem of Pound's historical record disappear simply because his poetry remains alive. “He spits in the mud and rubs it in the eyes of Ez Pound.” The third-person shift is striking. The person who asks who has the authority to forgive Pound also becomes someone who performs a hostile, bodily action against him. Forgiveness and aggression coexist. The poem's ending moves into a landscape of Plutos, bones, rocks, and writing on a wall. It concludes with the imperative “Leap!” That final command moves the poem away from resolving the ethical question in prose. The speaker must act, even though the terms of his relationship with his predecessor remain unsettled. I would pay particular attention to the title's use of “who.” It doesn't ask whether Pound can be forgiven; it asks who has the authority to do the forgiving. It then shifts into a narrated science-fiction action sequence. [chip: Goodreads +1] The opening's syntax is important. It begins with a command to a system to recreate a history, but the request itself is already highly stylized: the reader is asked to receive an epic account of events that supposedly belong to the future. Then comes the single-word transition: “Commence:” The word functions almost like a stage direction or a computer instruction. It ends the invocation and begins the story proper. The poem's temporal structure is also unusual. The heading claims that the fragment was recovered from the future, while its introductory note places it after a dream. The text therefore presents itself as a document whose origin lies on the other side of ordinary chronology. This raises a question about the relationship between epic and science fiction. Both forms can organize individual lives around immense historical processes: the fate of a civilization, a war, a journey, or the survival of a people. Here, the System is asked to perform a role comparable to that of an epic singer, preserving a story whose scale exceeds the individual protagonist. The poem also makes the archive itself part of the fiction. The work is not simply about the future; it is presented as a recovered artifact from that future. That framing asks us to consider what makes a text appear authoritative: its contents, its purported origin, or the narrative that explains how it came to be preserved. 9.
